doc.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: What goes through his mind when improvising
summary: He describes having things to play, following how voices move, and above all knowing where you are in the song, which he teaches at Jay Unger's camp.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you were explaining to a person who knew music pretty well but just had no idea how musicians go about improvising, the thought process, when you’re playing on “Ain’t Misbehavin’” for instance, can you describe what you’re thinking while you’re playing?

Yeah, you know I’ve thought about that a lot since I’ve been teaching improvising. For the past four or five years, I’ve been teaching maybe three weeks a year at a camp run by a violinist named Jay Unger who does a lot of Ken Burns’ scores for like the “Civil War” and like that, and teaching people who can play but don’t improvise. It’s a combination of things. One is having things to play, like little stuff that you can play if you can’t think of anything better to play; then knowing not really the chords of the songs so much as how the voices move in the song. If you play a one note at a time instrument that’s really what you’re doing. You’re not thinking like C seven to F seven, although you know that’s going on, you’re thinking like what voice moves to which and how a note is going to sound in a particular harmonic setting as you’re playing along. And then what I tell my students is even more important than knowing every chord is knowing where you are in the song. I mean that’s really more important than anything.
Knowing the form and feeling where you’re at.
Did you ever have an occasion on any of these parties where that goes out the window?

Well there are certain tunes that are two sixteen bar patterns that are almost the same. And that can happen like during a drum solo or something, you really have to just remember where you are. But the musicians that do these parties are very good. I’d say that happens very rarely.
Rarely. Did you know every tune they played that first set?
